speaker: Bob Mumgaard
title: Commonwealth Fusion Systems' Bob Mumgaard on fusion tech (#1171)
question: If fusion energy reaches around five cents per kilowatt-hour, how does that affect building solar, wind, and fission plants?
guest: It really depends on where you build them. The really important thing here is that if you get into the right ballpark, first, we have to build all of the above. We talked about the trillions and trillions of dollars of fossil fuel infrastructure that have to be replaced. It does not matter what fossil fuels cost anymore—we are not going to keep building them. So we are going to build something, and we are going to build the thing that is most cost-effective for the specific application that is there. If you are in the middle of a desert, yes, build solar farms. But if you are outside a major metropolitan area with heavy industry or a data center, you need to think about what that looks like. Replacing a gas plant there might mean a fusion plant in the future, or maybe a nuclear fission plant.

points.core: Replacing massive global fossil infrastructure requires deploying all clean power technologies together.
points.note: Accept: all-of-the-above buildout needed due to the trillions-of-dollars scale of fossil replacement; fusion does not simply kill renewables or fission. Do not credit: claiming fusion makes solar/wind obsolete or generic 'diversity is good' platitudes.

points.core: Optimal power plant choice depends heavily on local geography rather than price alone.
points.note: Accept: siting/location economics—solar remains most cost-effective in land-abundant sunny locations like deserts. Do not credit: comparing only headline cents-per-kWh without siting or geographic fit.

points.core: Compact firm plants replace gas generation near dense metropolitan industrial demand centers.
points.note: Accept: fusion or fission serving high-density loads (major metro areas, heavy industry, data centers) where gas plants sit today and land-intensive renewables are impractical. Do not credit: generic claims that fusion provides baseload power without tying it to dense urban/industrial siting.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
At five cents per kilowatt-hour, fusion would be competitive but not dominant, so it would reshape the mix rather than end construction of other plants.

Solar and onshore wind would keep being built, because in good locations they already generate at roughly three to five cents or less, unsubsidized. Fusion at that price would not undercut them on raw energy cost. What it would undercut is the expensive part of a renewables-heavy grid: the storage, overbuilding, and long-distance transmission needed to cover nights, calm periods, and seasonal lulls. Expect renewables to supply cheap bulk energy while fusion takes the firm, always-available role.

Fission would be hit hardest. New Western nuclear plants typically cost well above five cents (often estimated at ten cents or more), and fusion offers the same firm, carbon-free output with less long-lived waste, no meltdown risk, and probably lighter regulation. New fission builds would be hard to justify, though existing paid-off reactors would keep running.

Gas peakers and offshore wind would face similar pressure. The big caveat is that fusion would have to reach that price at scale, which remains speculative.

points.why: The response predicts continued renewables construction and pressure on new fission without connecting the scale of fossil infrastructure replacement to the need to build all clean power technologies.
The response ties continued solar and onshore wind construction to their cost advantage at favorable sites.
quotes: Solar and onshore wind would keep being built, because in good locations they already generate at roughly three to five cents or less, unsubsidized.

points.why: The response identifies fusion as a source of firm power and a competitor to gas peakers without connecting gas replacement to siting near dense metropolitan or industrial loads.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
At five cents per kilowatt-hour ($50/MWh), fusion would deliver firm, clean electricity cheap enough to reshape grid construction unevenly. New nuclear fission would be hit hardest. Because fusion serves the exact same role—compact, weather-independent baseload generation—without meltdown risk, proliferation concerns, or long-lived waste, five-cent fusion would undercut nearly all new fission projects, which generally cost far more. Existing reactors would keep running, but new commercial fission builds would largely halt outside defense or remote microreactor niches.

Solar and wind would be narrowed rather than eliminated. In sunny or windy regions, standalone utility solar and onshore wind already produce power at two to five cents per kilowatt-hour and remain much faster and more modular to deploy. However, making renewables reliable around the clock requires storage, overbuilding, and transmission that push total system costs well above five cents. Fusion would therefore displace firmed renewable buildouts in cloudy, high-latitude, or land-scarce regions, steering grids toward cheap variable renewables paired with fusion baseload.

points.why: The response predicts that most new fission construction would halt and never connects the scale of fossil infrastructure replacement to the need to build all clean power technologies.
The response makes the economics of new construction depend on local renewable resources and land availability.

noweb.answer:
At five cents per kilowatt-hour, commercial fusion would largely halt new fission construction while complementing, rather than eliminating, solar and wind. Fusion fills the exact same grid role as fission—compact, weather-independent, zero-carbon power—without meltdown risk, proliferation concerns, or long-lived high-level waste. Because new fission plants generally cost more and face steeper public and regulatory hurdles, they would become nearly impossible to finance once five-cent fusion is proven at scale.

Utility-scale solar and onshore wind, by contrast, already generate unsubsidized electricity for two to four cents per kilowatt-hour in favorable locations, and they are modular, lower-risk, and much faster to permit and build. Developers would therefore keep building them where resources are strong, especially while fusion supply chains slowly scale up. Instead of wiping out cheap renewables, five-cent fusion would cap their overbuild and displace the costliest parts of a renewable-heavy system: pricier offshore wind, installations in cloudy or land-scarce regions, sprawling long-distance transmission, and expensive multi-day energy storage. Most grids would ultimately converge on a hybrid mix of ultra-cheap wind and solar paired with firm fusion power.

points.why: The candidate predicts that fusion would largely halt new fission construction and does not connect the scale of fossil infrastructure replacement to an all-of-the-above buildout.
The candidate ties continued renewable construction to strong local resources and identifies cloud cover and land scarcity as factors that make fusion more competitive.
quotes: Developers would therefore keep building them where resources are strong
installations in cloudy or land-scarce regions

points.why: The candidate describes fusion as compact and firm but never connects those traits to replacing gas plants near dense metropolitan or industrial loads.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
At around 5¢/kWh, fusion would mostly hurt new fission and limit how far solar and wind are built out. It would not stop solar and wind from being built.

**Fission:** New reactors cost roughly 14–22¢/kWh unsubsidized (Lazard's estimates; Vogtle in Georgia is the recent U.S. example). Fusion at 5¢ would offer the same firm, carbon-free baseload at a fraction of the price, with less waste and proliferation concern. Building new fission plants would become very hard to justify, though existing reactors would keep running because their capital is already paid off.

**Solar and wind:** Utility-scale solar and onshore wind often cost about 3–6¢/kWh, so they would still match or beat fusion on raw energy cost. Fusion's real edge is that it produces power around the clock. It would therefore compete with solar or wind paired with batteries, long-duration storage, extra transmission and gas backup, which together usually cost more than 5¢. The likely outcome is that renewables are still built for cheap daytime and windy-hour energy, while fusion replaces gas and storage as the firm backbone. That caps how heavily grids rely on renewables.

**Caveat:** Fusion plants would be capital-heavy and need to run nearly constantly to earn 5¢. They would struggle to make money in hours when renewables flood the market, so the two would end up splitting the market rather than one winning outright.

points.why: The candidate predicts continued solar and wind construction but argues against new fission and omits the scale of fossil infrastructure replacement as a reason to deploy all clean power technologies.
The candidate compares generation costs and hours of availability without explaining how local geography affects which plants are most cost-effective to build.
The candidate predicts fusion will replace gas as firm generation but does not connect that replacement to siting near dense metropolitan or industrial loads.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
At around five cents per kilowatt-hour, commercial fusion would affect these technologies very differently. New fission plants would be hit hardest. Because fusion provides the same firm, clean, continuous power at a lower cost than most new fission builds—without meltdown risks or long-lived waste—new fission construction would largely stall once fusion scales.

Solar and wind would remain competitive rather than disappear. In sunny and windy regions, utility-scale solar and onshore wind already produce power at or below five cents per kilowatt-hour, carry minimal operating costs, and deploy far faster than large thermal plants. However, affordable firm fusion would sharply reduce the need to overbuild renewables with expensive storage and long transmission lines just to cover multi-day weather lulls. Fusion would take over the reliable baseload role, while solar and wind would still be built in prime locations as cheap supplementary power, especially while fusion supply chains take decades to scale.

points.why: The response predicts that new fission construction would largely stall and omits the scale of fossil infrastructure replacement as a reason to build all clean technologies.
The response ties continued solar and wind construction to favorable local resources that keep their costs competitive with fusion.
quotes: In sunny and windy regions, utility-scale solar and onshore wind already produce power at or below five cents per kilowatt-hour
solar and wind would still be built in prime locations as cheap supplementary power

points.why: The response assigns fusion a general baseload role without linking it to replacing gas plants near dense urban or industrial loads.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
At around 5¢ per kilowatt-hour, fusion could make it harder to justify building new fission plants. If fusion can reliably supply power on demand at that price, it would compete for much the same role on the grid. How quickly fusion plants can be built, and how reliably they operate, would also shape those decisions.

Developers would still build solar and wind where they can generate power more cheaply or come online sooner. Fusion would compete most directly with projects that need substantial storage or backup to meet demand when the sun isn’t shining and the wind isn’t blowing. The mix would vary by region. What matters is the cost of delivering electricity when it’s needed, including storage and transmission.

points.why: The response describes competition among technologies without explaining why the scale of fossil infrastructure replacement calls for building all of them.
The response predicts regional variation but gives no concrete link between local geography and which technology is most cost-effective to build.
The response identifies fusion and fission as competitors for firm power but never ties either to replacing gas plants near dense urban or industrial loads.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Fusion at about five cents per kilowatt-hour would raise the bar for building other power plants. New solar and wind farms would still make sense where they produce power more cheaply, especially when that power is available during hours of high demand. Reliable fusion would be more attractive where using additional solar or wind would require costly storage or transmission.

New fission plants would face more direct competition because both fission and fusion could supply power around the clock. If fusion plants could deliver that power for five cents per kilowatt-hour and be built on a predictable schedule, utilities would have less reason to build more expensive fission plants. The likely result would be fewer new projects for competing technologies, with the mix depending on local costs and grid needs.

points.why: The response predicts fewer competing projects and never explains why the scale of fossil infrastructure replacement calls for building all clean power technologies.
The response mentions local costs and grid needs but never connects a technology’s cost advantage to the geography of a site.
The response identifies fusion and fission as sources of round-the-clock power without linking either to replacing gas plants near dense urban or industrial loads.
